source.title: Emergent Inverse-Depth Scaling From Nonlinearity In Attention
source.authors: Zi-Rui Peng; Yizhou Liu; Zi-Ming Liu; Jeff Gore

record.tranche_reason: Tests loss scaling with depth in controlled in-context-learning tasks and generalized Transformer-like variants, rather than scaling with parameter count, tokens, or compute in language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The study measures evaluation MSE against depth on synthetic ICL tasks. It does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy against parameter count, tokens, or training compute. Loss-floor comparisons, attention-mass diagnostics, and the layerwise error decomposition explain the reported scaling but are not separate scaling-law rows here.
record.test_reason: Width is fixed, so parameters grow linearly with depth. Converged evaluation MSE versus depth in toy attention models on synthetic in-context-learning regression is therefore a parameter-scaling result in a non-text training regime (V5). It is not language-model pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute, so V1–V4, V6 and V7 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors also show linear attention follows a spectrum-dependent depth power law on the easy task and plateaus on the difficult task. They argue nonlinear attention makes depth scaling less dependent on data covariance, while stressing toy-model and ICL-only limits.
record.recipe_differences: Controlled synthetic ICL regression and retrieval tasks; measures MSE over depth, not language-model pretraining cross-entropy over parameter count, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Scaling behavior varies with target aggregation: top-2 retains an inverse-depth signal with context updates, whereas top-16 quickly saturates. Top-16 fitted exponents also differ more from one over the tested depth range.

fits_no_version.finding: In the controlled nonlinear-attention model, the depth exponent is about 1 (inverse depth) across data spectra. The authors attribute it to ensemble-like averaging across layers, with the shared error setting the floor.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At fixed width, the reducible loss of attention models falls roughly as 1/depth, independent of data spectrum.

record.problems: Experiments use synthetic ICL tasks and a simplified architecture; experiments on generalized architectures cover a smaller accessible depth range and are described as scaling signals rather than definitive asymptotic evidence. The study does not address coupling of depth scaling to model width or dataset size.
record.rows_left_out: Did not include separate rows for linear-attention easy-task power-law fits, linear-attention difficult-task plateaus, loss-floor comparisons, or attention diagnostics. These chiefly compare mechanisms or characterize floors rather than test the selected V5 result on nonlinear-attention depth scaling; see Sections 3-4, Tables 1-3, and Appendices A and D.2.

untested.parts: Image, video and other real modalities; repeated data; fine-tuning and transfer; scaling in data, tokens or compute; width scaling. Only depth (with width fixed) on synthetic ICL regression is tested.
Pretraining cross-entropy of language models versus parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolation from small to much larger runs.
Depth versus width at a fixed parameter count.
Sensitivity of fitted laws to setup or fitting choices in LM pretraining.

missing.what: Nonlinear attention on the easy task: one layer reaches zero loss and extra depth gives no further gain, so no depth scaling appears.

record.verdict_notes: The V5 link is generous: the toy synthetic-regression depth scaling is only loosely a 'training regime' for LM scaling laws. rows_left_out declares the linear-attention easy-task fits (Table 2, α 1.12–3.31) and difficult-task plateaus (Fig. 5, Table 3). These do bear on V5 (one power-law observed, one absent) and should become rows. Top-16 'partial' states were judged against inverse-depth, not against V5.

versions.untested_parts: No loss sweep against parameter count, training tokens, or compute.
No prediction of much larger runs from fits to smaller runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep over parameter count and tokens.
The study compares attention nonlinearities and relaxes architectural assumptions, but does not measure loss changes from depth, width, or other architecture details at a fixed parameter count.
Tests depth-dependent loss scaling in synthetic ICL tasks, not other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, transfer, or standard text-pretraining regimes.
No downstream task performance or relationship between downstream performance and pretraining loss.
Reports a fitting procedure and varies task spectra and targets, but does not test how fitted laws change under alternative fitting methods, parameter-counting choices, or pretraining setups.
